title: Best Plant Protein Sources: How Much They Provide per Serving

seo.title: Best Plant Protein Sources by Serving
seo.meta_description: Compare tempeh, tofu, seitan, beans, lentils, nuts and seeds by protein per realistic serving and learn how to build high-protein plant meals.
seo.search_intent: Find practical plant protein sources and compare realistic serving amounts.

excerpt: Tempeh, tofu, seitan, soybeans and legumes are easy to use as the protein center of a plant-based meal. Nuts and seeds add protein, but their usual servings are smaller.
content_html:
A vegetarian or vegan diet can easily provide enough protein when meals regularly include a recognizable protein source. Soy foods, seitan and legumes work especially well because they can be eaten in substantial portions; nuts and seeds are more concentrated by weight but usually eaten in smaller amounts.

Practical plant protein sources

FoodServingApprox. protein
Seitan5 oz / 142 g28–33 g
Tempeh5 oz / 142 g~28 g
Cooked soybeans1 cup / ~170 g~31 g
Firm tofu6 oz / 170 g~20–28 g depending on brand
Cooked lentils1 cup / ~200 g18 g
Cooked chickpeas1 cup / ~200 g~18 g
Cooked edamame1 cup / ~155 g~18 g
Hemp seeds1 oz / 28 g~9 g
Peanuts1 oz / 28 g~7 g

Soy foods

Cooked mature soybeans provide about 18.2 g protein per 100 g, roughly twice the 9 g in cooked lentils. Soy also has one of the strongest essential-amino-acid profiles among plant foods.

Tempeh is near 20 g/100 g, while tofu varies with water content. Firm or extra-firm tofu can contain far more protein than silken tofu, so the nutrition label is useful when protein is a priority.

Seitan

Seitan is made from wheat gluten and commonly provides 20–25 g protein per 100 g. It is relatively low in lysine compared with legumes and soy, so a diet that also contains those foods creates a better overall amino-acid balance.

Seitan is not appropriate for people with celiac disease.

Beans and lentils

Cooked lentils, chickpeas and beans are generally around 8–9 g protein per 100 g. A 1-cup portion of lentils provides about 18 g protein plus roughly 15–16 g fiber.

By comparison, the same 200 g weight of cooked chicken breast would exceed 60 g protein but supply no fiber. Legumes contribute less concentrated protein while adding fiber, folate, potassium and nonheme iron.

Textured vegetable protein

Dry textured soy protein can exceed 45–50 g protein per 100 g because it contains very little water. If 2 ounces / 56 g dry product is 50% protein, the meal receives about 28 g protein even after the product absorbs water and becomes much heavier.

Nuts and seeds

Hemp and pumpkin seeds are around 30 g protein per 100 g, while peanuts are about 25.8 g. A normal 1-ounce portion provides roughly 9 g from hemp and 7 g from peanuts.

They are excellent additions, but using almonds alone to obtain 30 g protein would require roughly 5 ounces / 140 g, far more than a typical serving and a substantial amount of calories.

Grains contribute too

Dry oats provide around 12–13 g protein per 100 g, so a 60 g bowl contributes about 7–8 g. Bread, pasta, rice and quinoa also count toward the daily total even when they are not the main protein source.

What about quinoa?

Cooked quinoa is around 4–5 g protein per 100 g, well below lentils, tofu or tempeh. It has a favorable amino-acid profile for a plant food, but it is not exceptionally protein-dense.

Building a 25–35 g plant-protein meal

MealApprox. protein
5 oz tempeh + rice + vegetables30–35 g
6 oz firm tofu + 1/2 cup edamame30–40 g depending on tofu
1 cup lentils + whole-grain bread + seeds25–30 g
Oats + soy milk + peanut butter + hemp seeds20–30 g depending on amounts

Complete proteins and combining

Plant proteins do not need to be paired at every meal. Eating soy foods, legumes, grains, nuts and seeds across the day provides complementary amino-acid patterns. Total protein and variety matter more than rigid food pairing.

Vitamin B12

A vegan diet can be high in protein and still require deliberate vitamin B12 intake. Ordinary plant foods are not reliable B12 sources, so fortified foods and/or supplementation are necessary.

Bottom line

Soy, tofu, tempeh, seitan and legumes make the strongest anchors for protein-rich plant meals. Nuts, seeds and grains add useful amounts and broaden the nutritional profile.

Sources

Food composition values come from USDA FoodData Central. Protein-quality concepts come from FAO.

faq.question: What is the best plant protein source?
faq.answer: For main meals, soy foods, tempeh, tofu, seitan and legumes are especially practical. Tempeh and seitan can provide around 30 g per 5-ounce serving.

faq.question: Do plant proteins need to be combined in one meal?
faq.answer: No. Variety across the day provides amino-acid complementarity.

faq.question: Is quinoa very high in protein?
faq.answer: Cooked quinoa has roughly 4–5 g/100 g, less than lentils, tofu or tempeh.
